main.summary: Su Xun argues that the six states fell not because their weapons were poor or their fighting bad, but because they bought Qin off with land and gifts, which steadily drained their own strength. He uses the past to warn the Song not to bow to foreign enemies with yearly payments.
main.translation:
The six states were broken and destroyed, not because their weapons were not sharp or their fighting not good: the flaw lay in bribing Qin. Bribing Qin drained their strength, and that was the road to ruin.
Someone may say: 'The six states ruined one another in turn - was it all because they bribed Qin?' I say: those who did not bribe were ruined because of those who did; having lost a strong ally, they could not stand intact alone. That is why I say the flaw lay in bribing Qin.
Besides what Qin gained by attack, it took a town when the gain was small and a city when it was large. If you compare what Qin got in this way with what it got by winning battles, it is in truth a hundred times more; and what the lords lost in this way, compared with what they lost by being beaten in battle, is also in truth a hundred times more. So what Qin most desired and what the lords most dreaded were really not in the fighting at all.
Think of their ancestors: they stood in frost and dew and cut down thorns and brambles to have a few feet and inches of land. Their descendants looked on it without much regret, and gave it all to others as if throwing away straw. Today they cut off five cities, tomorrow ten, and only then do they get one night of sound sleep. They rise and look at the four borders, and the soldiers of Qin have come again. The lords' land is limited, and the violence of Qin is never satisfied; the more is offered, the harder it presses. So before any fighting, the question of strong and weak, win and lose, was already decided. That they ended in overthrow is only what we should expect. The ancients said: 'To serve Qin with land is like carrying firewood to put out a fire: until the firewood is gone, the fire will not die.' These words are right.
The people of Qi never bribed Qin, yet in the end they followed the other five in being moved and destroyed. Why? Because they sided with Qin and did not help the five. When the five were lost, Qi could not escape either. The rulers of Yan and Zhao at first had far-sighted plans and were able to keep their land, and in justice they did not bribe Qin. For that reason Yan, though a small state, fell later, and this was the result of resisting by arms. When it came to Prince Dan taking Jing Ke as his plan, disaster came quickly. Zhao fought Qin five times, losing twice and winning three times. Later, when Qin attacked Zhao twice more, Li Mu drove them back each time. When Li Mu was put to death on slander, Handan became a Qin commandery; it is a pity that they used force and did not keep it up to the end. Besides, Yan and Zhao were facing Qin just as it had almost wiped out the others, and their wisdom and strength were isolated and endangered; being beaten and destroyed was truly unavoidable.
Had the three states each cherished their land, had Qi not attached itself to Qin, had the assassin not gone, and had the good general still been alive, then the count of wins and losses, and the matter of survival and ruin, set against Qin, might not have been easy to calculate. Alas! If the land given to bribe Qin had been used to enfeoff the schemers of the world, and the heart used to serve Qin had been used to honour the remarkable talents of the world, and they had joined their strength and faced west, then I fear the people of Qin could not have swallowed their food. How sad!
With such strength, they were seized by the long-built power of Qin, cut away day by day, month by month, until they headed for ruin. Let those who rule states not be held hostage by built-up power! The six states and Qin were all lords, and their strength was less than Qin's, yet they still had the means to win without bribery. If a realm as great as the empire follows the old path of the six states' ruin, it will be even lower than the six states!

keyLines.line: 六國破滅，非兵不利，戰不善，弊在賂秦
keyLines.en: The six states were broken and destroyed, not because their weapons were not sharp or their fighting not good: the flaw lay in bribing Qin.
keyLines.note: He states the central point at the outset: the root of the six states' ruin was bribing Qin.

keyLines.line: 古人云：「以地事秦，猶抱薪救火，薪不盡，火不滅。」
keyLines.en: To serve Qin with land is like carrying firewood to put out a fire: until the firewood is gone, the fire will not die.
keyLines.note: He quotes an old saying as a comparison: giving up land to buy peace only enlarges the disaster.

keyLines.line: 今日割五城，明日割十城，然後得一夕安寢。起視四境，而秦兵又至矣
keyLines.en: Today they cut off five cities, tomorrow ten, and only then do they get one night of sound sleep. They rise and look at the four borders, and the soldiers of Qin have come again.
keyLines.note: It sets the rulers' craving for ease against the return of Qin's soldiers, and shows vividly how pointless it is to give away land.

keyLines.line: 秦之所大欲，諸侯之所大患，固不在戰矣
keyLines.en: So what Qin most desired and what the lords most dreaded were really not in the fighting at all.
keyLines.note: He points out that Qin's true aim, and the lords' true misfortune, lay in the land they gave up, not in war.

keyLines.line: 是故燕雖小國而後亡，斯用兵之效也
keyLines.en: For that reason Yan, though a small state, fell later, and this was the result of resisting by arms.
keyLines.note: Yan is used as a positive example of resistance, to bring out the mistake of bribing Qin.

keyLines.line: 以賂秦之地，封天下之謀臣；以事秦之心，禮天下之奇才
keyLines.en: If the land given to bribe Qin had been used to enfeoff the schemers of the world, and the heart used to serve Qin had been used to honour the remarkable talents of the world.
keyLines.note: He puts forward a supposition: if what was spent on bribing Qin had gone to talented men, they could have joined forces against Qin.

keyLines.line: 為國者無使為積威之所劫哉
keyLines.en: Let those who rule states not be held hostage by built-up power!
keyLines.note: The conclusion of the essay: a warning to rulers not to be cowed by an enemy's long-accumulated power.

keyLines.line: 苟以天下之大，而從六國破亡之故事，是又在六國下矣
keyLines.en: If a realm as great as the empire follows the old path of the six states' ruin, it will be even lower than the six states!
keyLines.note: He turns to the Song: if it repeats the old mistake, it will be worse than the six states.

glossary.note: To give up land and send goods to Qin to buy a quiet life.
A strong ally or source of help.
An old word meaning 'their' (the lords' own).

glossary.en: bao shuang lu, zhan jing ji - exposed to frost, cutting thorns
glossary.note: Standing in frost and dew and cutting thorns; the hardship of the ancestors in founding their states.
Jing Ke, whom Prince Dan of Yan sent to try to assassinate the King of Qin.
A famous general of Zhao who drove back the armies of Qin several times and was later ruined by slander.
To destroy; it refers to Qin swallowing up the other states.
The might that has been accumulated over a long time.

main.background: Su Xun (1009-1066) was a prose writer of the Northern Song (960-1127) and one of the 'Eight Masters of the Tang and Song'. This essay is from his Quan shu. In discussing how the six states perished by bribing Qin, it criticises the Song policy of buying peace from the Liao and the Western Xia with yearly payments, and is a famous piece of historical argument.
